questions.question: What does the name of Spain's "AVE" high-speed train stand for?
questions.fact: The first AVE line, Madrid to Seville, opened in April 1992, just in time for Seville's Expo '92.

questions.question: Which Spanish city's metro opened first, in 1919?
questions.fact: King Alfonso XIII opened the first line, from Sol to Cuatro Caminos, on 17 October 1919. Barcelona's metro followed in 1924.

questions.question: What is the name of Spain's state-owned train operator?
questions.fact: Since 2021 Renfe's high-speed trains have faced rivals Ouigo and Iryo on routes like Madrid to Barcelona, pushing ticket prices down.

questions.question: Which Spanish train, designed by engineer Alejandro Goicoechea, is famous for its light articulated carriages?
questions.fact: Talgo stands for "Tren Articulado Ligero Goicoechea Oriol", after the engineer and his backer, José Luis Oriol.

questions.question: Which small SEAT model, launched in 1957, became a symbol of Spain's economic boom?
questions.fact: Nicknamed "pelotilla", it was built under licence from Fiat. Around 800,000 were made before production ended in 1973.

questions.question: Which SEAT spin-off brand became a separate sporty car maker in 2018?
questions.fact: The name is short for "Cup Racing", a nod to SEAT's motorsport history. The brand is based in Martorell, near Barcelona, like SEAT.

questions.question: Which luxury car maker, founded in Barcelona in 1904, also built aircraft engines?
questions.fact: The name means "Spanish-Swiss": its star engineer, Marc Birkigt, came from Switzerland. King Alfonso XIII was a keen customer.

questions.question: Which car brand's logo is a three-pointed star?
questions.fact: The three points are said to stand for the company's aim of powering transport on land, at sea and in the air.

questions.question: Which country does the car maker Volvo come from?
questions.fact: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin invented the three-point seat belt in 1959, and Volvo let other car makers use the patent for free.

questions.question: What does "Volkswagen" mean in German?
questions.fact: Over 21 million original Beetles were built. The very last one rolled off the line in Puebla, Mexico, in 2003.

questions.question: Which Ford car, made from 1908 to 1927, was nicknamed the "Tin Lizzie"?
questions.fact: Henry Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, cut the time to build one from about 12 hours to about an hour and a half.

questions.question: Which car brand is most associated with James Bond, starting with the DB5 in "Goldfinger"?
questions.fact: The film DB5 had a passenger ejector seat. One of the original gadget-fitted DB5s sold at auction for about 6.4 million dollars in 2019.

questions.question: What does BMW stand for in English?
questions.fact: BMW began by making aircraft engines. The idea that its logo shows a spinning propeller came from a 1929 advert, not its original design.

questions.question: Which French car maker has a lion as its logo?
questions.fact: Peugeot started in the 1800s making tools, coffee grinders and pepper mills, and it still sells pepper mills today.

questions.question: Which French car was famously designed to carry a basket of eggs across a ploughed field without breaking any?
questions.fact: "2CV" means "two horsepower", a French tax rating, not its real power. It was built from 1948 to 1990.

questions.question: Which car maker drove a car based on its Chiron at over 300 mph (483 km/h) in 2019?
questions.fact: Bugatti was founded in 1909 by Italian-born Ettore Bugatti in Molsheim, Alsace, then part of Germany and now in France.

questions.question: What is the name of the winged figure on the bonnet of a Rolls-Royce?
questions.fact: It was reportedly modelled on Eleanor Thornton, secretary to an early motoring enthusiast. On modern cars it can retract into the grille.

questions.question: Which steam locomotive set the world speed record for steam, 203 km/h, in 1938?
questions.fact: Mallard's record of 126 mph still stands for steam. The locomotive is kept at the National Railway Museum in York.

questions.question: Which locomotive, built by George and Robert Stephenson, won the Rainhill Trials in 1829?
questions.fact: On the opening day of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830, Rocket hit and killed MP William Huskisson.

questions.question: Which country's "bullet train", the Shinkansen, opened in 1964?
questions.fact: It opened just before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. Its average delay is famously measured in seconds rather than minutes.

questions.question: What is the world's longest railway tunnel?
questions.fact: The Swiss tunnel is about 57 km long, opened in 2016, and runs up to 2,300 m beneath the peaks of the Alps.

questions.question: Which is the world's longest railway line, running from Moscow to Vladivostok?
questions.fact: The main route covers about 9,289 km. Travelling it without stopping takes around a week.

questions.question: Which famous luxury train ran from Paris to Istanbul?
questions.fact: It first ran in 1883 and inspired Agatha Christie's 1934 novel "Murder on the Orient Express".

questions.question: Madrid's Chamberí metro station is famous for being what?
questions.fact: Closed in 1966 because its curved platform was too short for longer trains, it reopened in 2008 as a museum with its original tiles and ads.

questions.question: What is the general speed limit for cars on Spanish motorways, in km/h?
questions.fact: France and Italy allow 130 km/h on motorways, while much of Germany's Autobahn has only an advisory limit of 130.

questions.question: Since 2021, what is the speed limit on Spanish town streets with one lane each way, in km/h?
questions.fact: Spain was one of the first countries to make 30 km/h the general urban limit. Streets with two or more lanes each way stay at 50.

questions.question: What shape is a European "Stop" sign?
questions.fact: Its unique eight-sided shape lets drivers recognise it even from behind, or when snow or dirt covers the word.

questions.question: In Europe, what does a blue circular road sign usually tell you?
questions.fact: Under the 1968 Vienna Convention, red-bordered circles forbid, blue circles order, triangles warn and rectangles inform.

questions.question: What background colour do motorway signs have in Spain?
questions.fact: In Italy and Switzerland it's the reverse: motorway signs are green, while ordinary main-road signs are blue.

questions.question: In Spain, what is the "ITV" for a car?
questions.fact: A private car needs its first ITV at four years old, then every two years, and every year once it's over ten.

questions.question: Which DGT environmental sticker do fully electric cars get in Spain?
questions.fact: The blue "Cero" label lets cars enter low-emission zones in cities like Madrid and Barcelona, where older unlabelled cars face bans.

questions.question: Which supersonic airliner carried passengers from 1976 to 2003?
questions.fact: At twice the speed of sound, Concorde could fly from London to New York in about three and a half hours.

questions.question: What is the world's largest passenger airliner?
questions.fact: The double-decker is certified for over 850 passengers in an all-economy layout, though airlines usually fit around 500.

questions.question: Airbus has its headquarters near which French city?
questions.fact: Airbus parts are built across Europe, including at Getafe and Illescas in Spain, and wings at Broughton in Wales.

questions.question: Who made the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in 1927?
questions.fact: His plane, the "Spirit of St. Louis", had a big fuel tank where the windscreen would be, so he used a periscope to see ahead.

questions.question: Who made the first aeroplane flight across the English Channel, in 1909?
questions.fact: He won a 1,000-pound prize from the Daily Mail, flying from near Calais to Dover in about 37 minutes.

questions.question: What is the three-letter code for Madrid-Barajas airport?
questions.fact: Barajas's Terminal 4, by Richard Rogers and Estudio Lamela, won Britain's Stirling Prize for architecture in 2006.

questions.question: What is the left side of a ship called, when facing forward?
questions.fact: "Starboard" comes from "steer board": old ships were steered by an oar on the right, so they tied up with their left side to the port.

questions.question: Which ship carried Charles Darwin around the world from 1831?
questions.fact: Darwin was badly seasick for much of the five-year voyage and spent as much time as he could exploring on land.

questions.question: Which ship completed the first voyage around the world in 1522, under Juan Sebastián Elcano?
questions.fact: Of five ships and around 240 men who set out from Spain in 1519, only the Victoria and 18 men made it back.

questions.question: Who built the "running machine" in 1817, an early bicycle with no pedals?
questions.fact: Some historians link it to 1816's "year without a summer", when failed harvests made horses costly to feed.

questions.question: What was the early bicycle with a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel called?
questions.fact: It was named after the large British penny and small farthing coins. The pedals were fixed to the big wheel, so bigger meant faster.

questions.question: How many points does the winner of a Formula 1 Grand Prix get?
questions.fact: A win has been worth 25 points since 2010. Before that, a win earned just 10 points.

questions.question: In Formula 1, what does the chequered flag mean?
questions.fact: Other flags: yellow warns of danger, blue tells a driver to let a faster car pass, and red stops the session.

questions.question: Which team has won the most Formula 1 constructors' championships?
questions.fact: Ferrari is the only team to have raced in every Formula 1 World Championship season since it began in 1950.

questions.question: Which driver shares the record of seven F1 world titles with Michael Schumacher?
questions.fact: Hamilton won six of his titles with Mercedes, then moved to Ferrari in 2025 after 12 seasons with the German team.

questions.question: Which Spanish driver won his first Formula 1 race at Silverstone in 2022?
questions.fact: His father, Carlos Sainz Sr, has won the Dakar Rally four times, most recently in 2024 at the age of 61.

questions.question: Which country has the second-longest high-speed rail network in the world, after China?
questions.fact: Spain has nearly 4,000 km of high-speed lines, more than any other country in Europe. China's network is over ten times bigger.

questions.question: Which city has the world's oldest underground railway, opened in 1863?
questions.fact: The first line, the Metropolitan Railway, used steam locomotives in its tunnels, which made them famously smoky.

questions.question: On Spanish road signs, what does "AP" mean in a road number like AP-7?
questions.fact: Many Spanish tolls ended when concessions expired: the AP-7 between Alicante and Tarragona became free in 2020.

questions.question: What unit is a ship's speed measured in?
questions.fact: One knot is one nautical mile (1,852 m) per hour. Sailors once measured speed with a knotted rope tied to a floating log.

questions.question: Which Italian company makes the Vespa scooter?
questions.fact: "Vespa" means "wasp" in Italian, reportedly because of the scooter's buzzing engine and narrow-waisted shape.

questions.question: Which German airship caught fire while landing in New Jersey in 1937?
questions.fact: Remarkably, 62 of the 97 people on board survived the fire, which destroyed the airship in little more than half a minute.

questions.question: Which of these EU countries drives on the left?
questions.fact: Malta and Cyprus are the other EU countries that drive on the left. Sweden switched to the right overnight in 1967.

questions.question: Who patented the first practical petrol-powered car, in 1886?
questions.fact: In 1888 his wife Bertha Benz drove it about 100 km to visit her mother, without telling him: the first long car journey.

questions.question: Which road safety device did Percy Shaw invent in 1934?
questions.fact: By one popular account, he got the idea when his headlights lit up the eyes of a cat on a dark, foggy road.

questions.question: Where was the world's first traffic light installed, in 1868?
questions.fact: It was a gas-lit signal outside the Houses of Parliament, worked by a policeman. It exploded within weeks, injuring its operator.

questions.question: Which car broke the sound barrier on land in 1997?
questions.fact: RAF pilot Andy Green drove it at 1,228 km/h (763 mph) in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, a land speed record that still stands.

questions.question: How does Spain's traditional "Iberian" rail gauge compare with the European standard?
questions.fact: Iberian gauge is 1,668 mm against the standard 1,435 mm. AVE lines use the standard, and Talgo built axles that change gauge on the move.

questions.question: Which Spanish brand built lorries, buses and the Z-102 sports car in the 1950s?
questions.fact: Pegaso, named after the winged horse Pegasus, was the brand of the state-owned company ENASA and is best known for its trucks.
